instructions: Peel the daikon and slice it into 1-inch rounds. Trim the sharp edges off each round and cut a shallow cross into one flat side. Put the rounds in a large pot, cover with cold water, bring to a boil, then simmer for 20 minutes. Drain.
Meanwhile, lower the eggs into a pot of boiling water and boil for 8 minutes. Transfer them to cold water, then peel.
Score the konnyaku in a crosshatch on one side and cut it into triangles. Boil it in water for 3 minutes, then drain.
Put the fish cakes in a colander and pour boiling water over them to rinse off the oil. Cut the larger pieces into bite-size pieces. Cut the atsuage into bite-size pieces and the hanpen in half.
Set a large wide pot over medium-high heat. Add 6 cups of water, the dashi granules, soy sauce, sake, mirin and salt and stir until the granules dissolve.
Add the daikon, konnyaku and eggs. Bring it to a boil, then turn the heat to low and simmer, uncovered, for 20 minutes.
Add the fish cakes and the atsuage and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the hanpen and simmer for 3 minutes.
Taste the broth. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Ladle the oden into bowls with some broth. Serve with the karashi in a small dish on the side.

To keep leftovers, let the pot cool with everything in the broth. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. Take out the eggs and konnyaku before freezing, and freeze the rest for up to 1 month. Reheat over low heat and don't let it boil, or the fish cakes go soft and the broth turns cloudy.
method_notes: Just One Cookbook simmers daikon, konnyaku and eggs in a seasoned dashi first, then adds the fish cakes and fried tofu, and finishes with the hanpen. RecipeTin Eats uses the same order with potatoes and a longer rest in the broth. This one follows Just One Cookbook, with dashi granules for the broth, no rice-cake pouches or kombu knots, and the karashi served on the side. It takes about an hour and a half on the stove, so it suits a big pot that keeps.
